descriptor: The largest land carnivore, a marine mammal that hunts seals from the drifting sea ice of the Arctic.

physical.fact: Its fur is not white: each hair is clear and unpigmented, and the skin beneath is black.

range.summary: Circumpolar across the Arctic sea ice in 20 subpopulations, from Hudson Bay and the Canadian archipelago to Alaska, Russia, Greenland and Svalbard.

regions.name: Western Hudson Bay
regions.note: About 618 bears in 2021, roughly half the 1987 estimate, as ice-free seasons lengthened.

regions.name: Southern Hudson Bay
regions.note: The southernmost polar bears, summering on the Ontario coast and islands of James Bay.

regions.name: Southern Beaufort Sea
regions.note: Low survival from 2004 to 2006 cut numbers by 25 to 50%, to about 900 bears in 2010.

regions.name: Chukchi Sea
regions.note: Shared by the US and Russia, about 2,937 bears in 2016 and judged likely stable.

regions.name: M'Clintock Channel
regions.note: Recovering from overhunting, rising from about 284 bears around 2000 to 716 by 2016.

regions.name: Baffin Bay
regions.note: Shared by Nunavut and Greenland, estimated at about 2,826 bears in 2013.

regions.name: Southeast Greenland
regions.note: Recognised in 2022 as a distinct group that hunts from glacier ice in fjords.

regions.name: Svalbard and Barents Sea
regions.note: A 2015 survey found about 973 bears in the Norwegian Barents Sea, with no decline detected yet.

regions.name: Kara and Laptev Seas
regions.note: Bears in the Russian Kara and Laptev seas have never been fully surveyed, so trends are unknown.

source.label: IUCN/SSC Polar Bear Specialist Group: subpopulation status table

rangeHistory.note: No polar bear subpopulation has disappeared, so no areas are marked lost; the danger shows as decline within the range.

source.label: IUCN/SSC Polar Bear Specialist Group proceedings (1993 to 2009) and Regehr et al. 2016

population.note: PBSG published only ranges from 1993 to 2009, so the estimate shown is the midpoint. Changes between these totals mostly reflect which surveys were included, not real change, and several Russian Arctic subpopulations have never been surveyed.

threats.title: Loss of sea ice
threats.detail: A warming Arctic shortens the ice season, cutting hunting time and lengthening fasts on land.

threats.title: Conflict with people
threats.detail: Bears stranded ashore for longer wander into towns and camps, and some are killed in defence of life.

threats.title: Pollution
threats.detail: Persistent industrial chemicals concentrate up the Arctic food web and build up in polar bear fat.

threats.title: Industry and shipping
threats.detail: Oil, gas and shipping expand as the ice retreats, bringing spill risk and disturbance near dens.

places.name: Churchill
places.note: Bears gather on the Hudson Bay shore each autumn waiting for the sea to freeze.

places.name: Wapusk National Park
places.note: One of the largest denning areas known; mothers and cubs emerge in late winter.

places.name: Svalbard
places.note: Expedition ships from Longyearbyen search the pack ice edge in summer.

places.name: Wrangel Island
places.note: A remote reserve with very high densities of maternity dens. Access is tightly restricted.

sightings.tip: Churchill peaks in October and November before Hudson Bay freezes. Svalbard cruises run in July and August, and Wapusk den tours run in February and March.

actions.title: Cut your carbon emissions
actions.detail: Sea ice loss driven by warming is the single biggest threat, so every reduction in emissions counts.

actions.title: Back strong climate policy
actions.detail: Vote for and support leaders who commit to rapid, binding emission cuts.

actions.title: Travel with regulated operators
actions.detail: Choose tours that follow local viewing rules and keep a safe distance from bears.

actions.title: Support polar bear research
actions.detail: Long-term population monitoring is expensive and relies on sustained funding.

orgs.name: IUCN SSC Polar Bear Specialist Group

summary.text: The polar bear is a large bear native to the Arctic and nearby areas. It is closely related to the brown bear, and the two species can interbreed. The polar bear is the largest extant species of bear and land carnivore by body mass, with adult males weighing 300–800 kg (660–1,760 lb). The species is sexually dimorphic, as adult females are much smaller. The polar bear is white or yellowish-furred with black skin and a thick layer of fat. It is more slender than the brown bear, with a narrower skull, longer neck and lower shoulder hump. Its teeth are sharper and more adapted to cutting meat. The paws are large and allow the bear to walk on ice and paddle in the water.
